passages.title: Living hope requires changed conduct and sincere love during present trials
passages.summary: Peter writes to chosen exiles in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. He blesses God for a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. An inheritance is kept in heaven for them. For a little while trials grieve them and test their faith like gold. The prophets searched for this salvation. The readers are to be holy, for they were redeemed with Christ’s precious blood. They are to love one another from the heart. They were born again through God’s word, which remains forever.
passages.uncertainty: The map gives no exact location to the unnamed or heavenly settings in First Peter.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson connects trials with living hope and belonging to God. Why does a secure inheritance lead into sincere love rather than private confidence alone?

contextNote.title: Living hope requires changed conduct and sincere love during present trials
contextNote.text: Verses 18–19 say the readers were redeemed with the blood of Christ. Verse 22 says they have purified their souls by obeying the truth. That purifying has an aim stated in the verse: sincere brotherly affection. Then the command follows: love one another from the heart, fervently. Verse 23 gives the ground for it. They were born again of seed that does not perish. Verses 24–25 contrast that with grass, which withers.

passages.title: A shared spiritual house stands beside unequal power and the refusal of revenge
passages.summary: Peter tells them to put away malice and to long for pure milk. They come to Christ, a living stone, and are built into a spiritual house. They are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, and a holy nation. They once were not a people and now are God’s people. As foreigners they should live well among the Gentiles. They should be subject to kings and governors for the Lord’s sake. Servants should be subject even to harsh masters. Christ suffered for them and left an example.
passages.uncertainty: The map gives no exact location to the unnamed or heavenly settings in First Peter.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson connects Christ's example with faithful conduct during trials. How does the refusal of revenge place judgment beyond the present power of harsh masters?

contextNote.title: A shared spiritual house stands beside unequal power and the refusal of revenge
contextNote.text: Verse 18 tells servants to submit even to harsh masters. Verse 20 says there is no credit in bearing a deserved beating. Bearing unjust suffering is what God commends. Verse 21 gives Christ as the example for that case. Verse 23 says what he did not do: he did not curse back or threaten. He entrusted himself to the one who judges justly. Verse 24 adds that he bore our sins in his body on the tree.

passages.title: Shared inheritance and gentle witness frame the argument about suffering and rescue
passages.summary: Wives are told to be subject to their husbands and to value a gentle spirit. Husbands are told to honor their wives as joint heirs of life. All should be compassionate and not repay evil for evil. Peter quotes a psalm about seeking peace. If they suffer for righteousness, they are blessed. They should be ready to answer anyone who asks about their hope. Christ suffered once, the righteous for the unrighteous. He spoke to the spirits in prison, and baptism now saves.
passages.uncertainty: The map gives no exact location to the unnamed or heavenly settings in First Peter.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson reads the imprisoned spirits through Christ's visit to the spirit world. Why must an answer about hope include humility and a good conscience?

contextNote.title: Shared inheritance and gentle witness frame the argument about suffering and rescue
contextNote.text: Verse 15 tells them to be ready with an answer about their hope. It adds the manner: with humility and fear. Verse 16 adds a third condition, a good conscience. The reason is practical. They are being spoken against as evildoers. A good way of life disappoints those who curse it. Verse 17 says suffering for doing good is better than for doing evil.

passages.title: Changed conduct needs shared service when former companions respond with insults
passages.summary: Peter says Christ suffered in the flesh, and the readers should have the same mind. They have spent enough time in the ways of the Gentiles. Former companions think it strange and speak evil of them. The end of all things is near, so they should be sober and pray. Above all they should love one another earnestly, for love covers many sins. They should be hospitable without grumbling and use their gifts to serve. They should not be surprised at the fiery trial. If anyone suffers as a Christian, he should not be ashamed.
passages.uncertainty: The map gives no exact location to the unnamed or heavenly settings in First Peter.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson connects teaching to the dead with God's just judgment. How do hospitality and received gifts make love practical during insult and pressure?

contextNote.title: Changed conduct needs shared service when former companions respond with insults
contextNote.text: Verse 4 says former companions now speak evil of the readers. The next verses turn to life inside the group. Verse 8 asks for earnest love, and verse 9 for hospitality without grumbling. Verse 10 gives the rule for every member. Each has received a gift and is to use it to serve others. The verse calls them managers of God’s grace, which takes many forms. Verse 11 names two kinds of gift: speaking and serving.

passages.title: Leadership by example and shared humility answer danger without ruling through fear
passages.summary: Peter writes to the elders as a fellow elder who saw Christ’s sufferings. They are to shepherd God’s flock willingly, not for gain. They are not to lord it over the flock but to be examples. When the chief Shepherd appears, they will receive a crown of glory. The younger should be subject to the elder, and all should be humble. They should cast their worries on God, who cares for them. The devil prowls like a roaring lion, and they should resist him. Peter writes through Silvanus and sends greetings from Babylon and from Mark.
passages.uncertainty: The map gives no exact location to the unnamed or heavenly settings in First Peter.

lds.text: How does the chief Shepherd's promised appearance limit the authority of present leaders?

contextNote.title: Leadership by example and shared humility answer danger without ruling through fear
contextNote.text: Verse 2 gives three contrasts for elders, and verse 3 is the third. They serve willingly, not under pressure. They serve eagerly, not for dishonest gain. They lead by example, not by lording it over the flock. The flock is called “those entrusted to you,” so it is not theirs. Verse 4 names the chief Shepherd, who will appear. Verse 5 then asks humility of everyone, elders included.

regions.name: Judea · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome removed Herod’s son Archelaus in 6 CE and made Judea a province. Its governor lived at Caesarea on the coast.
regions.detail: Governors Felix and Festus hold Paul at Caesarea (Acts 23–26). Acts 12 names an earlier ruler King Herod; historians call him Agrippa I.
regions.uncertainty: The shape joins Judea, Samaria, and Idumea. The province grew after 44 CE.

regions.name: Syria · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Syria a province in 64 BCE. It bordered the lands of Herod’s family on the north.
regions.detail: Believers are first called Christians at Antioch in Syria (Acts 11:26). Antioch sends out Barnabas and Saul in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Cilicia · approximate
regions.summary: Cilicia lay on the south coast of Asia Minor. Rome took it in 64 BCE.
regions.detail: Paul comes from Tarsus in Cilicia (Acts 21:39). He passes through Syria and Cilicia in Acts 15:41.
regions.uncertainty: The shape shows the eastern plain around Tarsus only.

regions.name: Cyprus · Roman province
regions.summary: Cyprus was a Roman province under a proconsul. Paphos was its capital.
regions.detail: Barnabas comes from Cyprus (Acts 4:36). He and Saul cross the island from Salamis to Paphos in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape follows the modern coast of the island.

regions.name: Galatia · Roman province
regions.summary: Augustus made Galatia a province in 25 BCE. Ancyra was its capital.
regions.detail: Paul writes to the assemblies of Galatia. Acts 13–14 places him at Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Pamphylia on the south coast belonged to Galatia for a time.

regions.name: Asia · Roman province
regions.summary: Asia was a rich Roman province in western Asia Minor. A proconsul governed it.
regions.detail: Paul teaches in Ephesus for two years (Acts 19:10). Revelation 1–3 writes to seven assemblies in Asia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Bithynia and Pontus · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome joined Bithynia and Pontus into one province on the Black Sea coast.
regions.detail: The Spirit keeps Paul from entering Bithynia (Acts 16:7). First Peter greets believers in Pontus and Bithynia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the coast lands.

regions.name: Cappadocia · Roman province
regions.summary: Cappadocia became a Roman province in 17 CE. Its capital was a city named Caesarea.
regions.detail: People from Cappadocia hear Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). First Peter 1:1 greets believers there.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. This Caesarea is not the port in Judea.

regions.name: Macedonia · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Macedonia a province in 146 BCE. The Via Egnatia crossed it from west to east.
regions.detail: A vision calls Paul to Macedonia (Acts 16:9). He teaches in Philippi, Thessalonica, and Beroea.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It includes Thessaly and Epirus, which the province held.

regions.name: Achaia · Roman province
regions.summary: Achaia covered southern Greece. Augustus made it a province apart from Macedonia.
regions.detail: Paul speaks in Athens and stays in Corinth (Acts 17–18). Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, hears a charge against him.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. The province’s islands are not marked.

regions.name: Crete · part of a Roman province
regions.summary: Rome governed Crete together with Cyrenaica in North Africa.
regions.detail: Paul’s ship shelters along Crete in Acts 27. Paul leaves Titus in Crete to appoint elders (Titus 1:5).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the island. Cyrenaica is not marked.

regions.name: Italy
regions.summary: Italy was the home region of Rome. It had a special status among Roman lands.
regions.detail: Paul lands at Puteoli and goes on to Rome (Acts 28). Hebrews 13:24 sends greetings from the Italians.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the peninsula.

chapterMaps.narrative: Peter writes to chosen exiles in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. He blesses God for a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. An inheritance is kept in heaven for them. For a little while trials grieve them and test their faith like gold. The prophets searched for this salvation. The readers are to be holy, for they were redeemed with Christ’s precious blood. They are to love one another from the heart. They were born again through God’s word, which remains forever.

chapterMaps.narrative: Peter tells them to put away malice and to long for pure milk. They come to Christ, a living stone, and are built into a spiritual house. They are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, and a holy nation. They once were not a people and now are God’s people. As foreigners they should live well among the Gentiles. They should be subject to kings and governors for the Lord’s sake. Servants should be subject even to harsh masters. Christ suffered for them and left an example.

chapterMaps.narrative: Wives are told to be subject to their husbands and to value a gentle spirit. Husbands are told to honor their wives as joint heirs of life. All should be compassionate and not repay evil for evil. Peter quotes a psalm about seeking peace. If they suffer for righteousness, they are blessed. They should be ready to answer anyone who asks about their hope. Christ suffered once, the righteous for the unrighteous. He spoke to the spirits in prison, and baptism now saves.

chapterMaps.narrative: Peter says Christ suffered in the flesh, and the readers should have the same mind. They have spent enough time in the ways of the Gentiles. Former companions think it strange and speak evil of them. The end of all things is near, so they should be sober and pray. Above all they should love one another earnestly, for love covers many sins. They should be hospitable without grumbling and use their gifts to serve. They should not be surprised at the fiery trial. If anyone suffers as a Christian, he should not be ashamed.

chapterMaps.narrative: Peter writes to the elders as a fellow elder who saw Christ’s sufferings. They are to shepherd God’s flock willingly, not for gain. They are not to lord it over the flock but to be examples. When the chief Shepherd appears, they will receive a crown of glory. The younger should be subject to the elder, and all should be humble. They should cast their worries on God, who cares for them. The devil prowls like a roaring lion, and they should resist him. Peter writes through Silvanus and sends greetings from Babylon and from Mark.
